title: Third Year Labs - Ising Model
text:
0.1 Project Overview
This project involves identifying clusters of like spins and measuring how their size, shape, and evolution depend on temperature, revealing how cluster geometry underlies critical behaviour in the 2D Ising model.

title: Third Year Labs - Ising Model
section: 0.2 Key Definitions Used in The Project
text:
0.2 Key Definitions Used in The Project

In this project, a cluster is defined as a connected component of nearest-neighbour spins with the same orientation on the lattice. Connectivity is determined purely by geometric adjacency, meaning that any neighbouring spins with the same sign belong to the same cluster. This definition matches the approach used in studies of cluster geometry such as Domb and Stoll, and allows direct measurement of cluster size, shape, and connectivity from simulation data. The physical significance of this definition is supported by the Fortuin–Kasteleyn representation of the Ising model, which shows that spin correlations correspond to probabilities of sites belonging to the same cluster, ensuring that these geometric clusters are directly linked to the underlying statistical physics of the system.

title: 3  Week 1 Overview
text:
3.0.0.1 Main Activities:

Deciding direction of the project and possible avenues to explore.

The current top suggests are something to do with how clustering attributes (such as shapes and sizes) vary with dimensionality, or something to do with the critical exponent.
We are also looking into where there might be a cross over between the critical exponent and clustering attributes, and whether this could be incorporated into the project.

Setting up infrastructure to facilitate the project

Set up a GitHub account so that I could pull the start-up code repository
Installed Quarto, found I didn’t need to install Quarto and then set up Quarto access to work through Visual Studio Editor. VS Editor had to be deleted and re-installed, following which Quarto functioned.
I then set up a few pages on the website to become familiar with how it works.

Literature Inquiry

Searched online for articles on Cluster Algorithms and the Critical Exponent. I found several articles that were potentially of interested, including one that looked like it may contain helpful coding hints.
I ensured that all of the article were proper science articles from reputable sources.

Literature Review

I then proceeded to read the articles and write a (relatively!) brief literature review for each one.
One of the key observations from this was the way in which a Cluster is defined. I also established important equations and identified recommended approaches.
I then wrote a final literature summary and identified a possible project direction based on the content of the articles.




3.0.0.2 Main Discoveries:

Possible Project direction considered at this point: As the spatial dimension increases, cluster formation in the Ising model changes qualitatively. In one dimension, clusters remain finite and their size distribution is exactly known, reflecting the absence of a phase transition. In higher dimensions, clusters grow, change shape, and become increasingly compact as the system approaches the critical temperature. These geometric changes are directly linked to diverging correlation lengths and critical scaling. Cluster-based representations and algorithms reveal that clusters are the fundamental objects governing both static and dynamic critical behaviour, explaining why cluster size, shape, and formation times depend sensitively on dimension.

title: 4  Week 2 Overview
text:
4.0.0.1 Main Activities:

Installed Spyder

Installed Spyder as a more effective IDE that was very compatible with GitHub.

Reimagined Quarto

Used terminal and quarto preview to facilitate the lab book, rather than running through VS Editor.

Edited and Developed Base Code

Edited and developed the code that was provided at the beginning of the project so that it was tailored to the project direction.

Created Code for the Clustering Algorithms

I created the core of the code for the clustering algorithm.
As a starting point, I decided to focus on the cluster size, shape and speed to converge, when very close to the critical temperature.
I am endeavouring, at this point, to try and establish the clustering attribute outcomes for 1D, 2D and 3D beginning with the 2D code.
I decided that it would be better to have a set code block for 1D, 2D and 3D, rather than a set code block for the attributes and then re-coding them every time for the dimension.
I also decided that it would be beneficial to use Monte-Carlo Metropolis methods rather than Wolff or Swendsen due to the definition of a cluster.
It was also important to establish the exact definition for a cluster.




4.0.0.2 Main Discoveries:

Code core written
Definition of a cluster established: In this project, a cluster is defined as a connected component of nearest-neighbour spins with the same orientation on the lattice. Connectivity is determined purely by geometric adjacency, meaning that any neighbouring spins with the same sign belong to the same cluster. This definition matches the approach used in studies of cluster geometry such as Domb and Stoll, and allows direct measurement of cluster size, shape, and connectivity from simulation data. The physical significance of this definition is supported by the Fortuin–Kasteleyn representation of the Ising model, which shows that spin correlations correspond to probabilities of sites belonging to the same cluster, ensuring that these geometric clusters are directly linked to the underlying statistical physics of the system.

My main consideration when doing this was how to put the inputs needed to vary with the dimensions, as well as which graphs would still produce correctly and which would need reconstructing.

Less needed changing for 1D - the only significant edit was how to graphically represent 1D shape.

Started to produce results

I started to produce a few preliminary results, starting with 2D.
I began with a very small cluster size to confirm that the code was functioning correctly.

I then moved on to increasing the cluster size, noting that larger cluster sizes matched more closely with the literature. A drawback to larger cluster sizes is the configuration time.
I decided it was better to get concrete results for 2D before moving onto other dimensions.
To this end, I varied the temperature and cluster size to produce a series of results.

Whilst the 2D code produced in week 5 was running, it was very slow to produce the 300x300 cluster, running with 20,000 steps.
I wrote the re-worked the code so that it would run in on block on Jupyter Notebook, as it seemed this could decrease run times.

I also added a section to the code to produce a plot for each temperature output, visually displaying
the cluster shape and largest cluster size.

Continued with Report Writing

Further to my previous report writing done for this project, I started to focus on the theory, methods, results and references sections.
For the theory / methods section, I have used the equations compiled in week 5, along with an overview of the coding methods used.

For the referencing, I have used mybib.com to produce the citations, using Vancouver referring.
I have decided to include these in the report as plain references, rather than employing the specific latex functionality, as previously that has been very unsuccessful.
Once the code has complied, I then began by inputting the figures into latex, ensuring that the sizing was uniform, orderly and optimal, from both readability and space-saving perspectives.
I then proceeded to write the captions for all of these graphs.
Given the limited space, I selected the cluster graphs that contained the most information and best assisted the narrative, and created a single plot to contain these 4 graphs.

Given this is the last week of experiments, I decided to finalise the lab book.
I ensured that the weekly log was complete and up-to-date, that the equations page was functioning and that the main page included relevant and completed information.
